worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule IV prescription was issued on 1 March authorizing five refills. The patient first had it dispensed on 5 March and used three refills at Pharmacy A. On 20 August she asks Pharmacy B to obtain it, and the transfer is completed on 22 August. On 10 September she asks Pharmacy B for the next refill. May Pharmacy B dispense it?
steps: Start with the two ceilings. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the date on which it was issued, so the window closes six months after 1 March. Counted the Massachusetts way, the day after issue is day one (247 CMR 9.04(10)), so 1 March itself is not counted.
Count the refills separately. Three of the five authorized refills have been used, so two remain and the five-refill ceiling is not the obstacle in this fact pattern.

Ask what the 22 August transfer changed. It moved the prescription without creating new refill authority and without restarting the issue-date clock, so the prescription reached Pharmacy B carrying the same 1 March issue date and the same two remaining refills.
Apply the clock on 10 September. The six-month period measured from 1 March has run, and unused authorized refills do not survive the time limit.
worked_examples.resolution: Pharmacy B may not dispense the refill; only a new prescription from the practitioner restores capacity. The scenario invites two errors at once: starting the six months at the 5 March first dispensing, and treating the two unused refills as authority that outlives the clock.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts patient's Schedule III prescription with refills remaining was transferred from Pharmacy A to Pharmacy B last month. She now asks Pharmacy C to obtain it from Pharmacy B, and mentions that Pharmacy B told her it would charge five dollars to send it and that she would have to telephone Pharmacy B herself. Pharmacies B and C do not share a prescription database.
steps: Identify the pathway. The prescription has already been dispensed and has refills remaining, so this is a refill-purpose transfer under 21 CFR 1306.25 rather than the initial-dispensing electronic transfer.

Apply the federal ceiling before the state duty. 1306.25(a) permits the refill-purpose transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information on a one-time basis only, and that transfer has already been used moving the prescription from A to B.

Test the exception. It is available only where the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database. B and C do not, so the alternative allowing transfer up to the maximum authorized refills is unavailable.

Do not read the Massachusetts duty as an override. 247 CMR 9.14(1) says when a pharmacy must transfer; 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure permissible only if allowable under state law, so state law can withhold a federally permitted transfer but cannot supply federal transfer capacity the federal rule withholds.

Separate the two complaints the patient actually raised. The fee and the legwork are governed by 247 CMR 9.14(3) and 9.14(2), which forbid a transfer fee and permit the pharmacy to act as the patient's agent; those rules are unaffected by the transfer count.
worked_examples.resolution: The second refill-purpose transfer is not available on these facts, and a new prescription is what moves the therapy to Pharmacy C. The five-dollar charge and the instruction that the patient make her own telephone call were both improper regardless. The trap is reading the Massachusetts duty to transfer on request as removing the federal one-time cap.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts patient asks Pharmacy C to obtain a Schedule VI prescription issued eight months ago with four refills remaining. It has already been transferred once, from Pharmacy A to Pharmacy B. Pharmacy C has a certified pharmacy technician on shift and the pharmacist on duty approves her doing the work. A colleague objects that the federal one-time limit forbids a second transfer and that only a pharmacist may execute one.
steps: Classify the drug first. Massachusetts Schedules I through V are the substances the federal schedules list (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a); 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(E)), and 105 CMR 700.002(F) puts in Schedule VI only prescription drugs included in no other schedule. A Schedule VI drug is therefore not one of the substances the federal Schedules III, IV and V list.

That settles the first objection. 21 CFR 1306.25 governs the transfer of Schedule III, IV and V prescription information, so it never reaches this prescription and its one-time cap has nothing here to limit.

Apply the state rule that does govern. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(a) puts a Schedule VI transfer on the same footing as a Schedule III-V transfer, and 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, which is a count of refills rather than a count of transfers.

Check the state ceilings that do exist. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transferring a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued, and eight months is inside that period. The refills themselves are also still usable, because 247 CMR 9.04(12) keeps a Schedule VI prescription valid, and refillable, for one year from issue.

Now the second objection. The federal requirement that a transfer be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists belongs to the federal pathways, which do not reach this prescription, and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) permits a certified pharmacy technician to perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.
worked_examples.resolution: Both halves of the colleague's objection fail: the second transfer is permitted and the technician may execute it with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is carrying a federal Schedule III-V mechanic across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription that no federal schedule reaches.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber transmits an electronic Schedule II prescription to retail Pharmacy A. The drug is out of stock and nothing has been dispensed. The patient asks Pharmacy A to send the prescription to retail Pharmacy B. A technician offers to print it and fax it across, and a colleague says a Schedule II prescription can never be moved between pharmacies.
steps: Rule out the wrong pathway. 21 CFR 1306.25 transfers prescription information for the purpose of refill dispensing, and this prescription has never been dispensed, so that rule is not the one in play.

Identify the right one. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) permits the transfer for initial dispensing of an electronic controlled-substance prescription between retail pharmacies, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.
Refuse the print-and-fax. The pathway requires the prescription to remain in electronic form and unaltered; converting it to another form defeats the transfer.

Refuse the technician's participation on this transfer. The federal pathway requires the transfer to be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, and the Massachusetts certified-technician transfer authority is confined to Schedule VI in any event.
Note what is not available here. This pathway carries no shared-database counterpart, so it stays one-time regardless of what record system the two pharmacies share.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer is lawful, but only electronically, pharmacist to pharmacist, and once. The colleague's flat rule is the error the scenario invites; a never-dispensed electronic Schedule II prescription has a transfer pathway even though the refill-transfer rule does not reach Schedule II.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule III or IV prescription may not be filled or refilled more than ______ after the date it was issued, and may not be refilled more than ______ times.
retrieval_prompts.answer: six months; five. Both limits are in 21 CFR 1306.22(a), and each is independent of the other.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which sovereign supplies the five-refill and six-month limits for a Schedule V prescription, and which facility type is excluded from them?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Massachusetts, at 247 CMR 9.04(13); the federal refill provision at 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is written for Schedules III and IV. 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that 9.04(13) does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the six-month clock starts running at the first dispensing, and it limits refills only.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False on both counts. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) and 247 CMR 9.04(13) each measure from the date the prescription was issued, and each bars filling as well as refilling once six months have passed, so a prescription that has never been dispensed is equally out of time. In Massachusetts the day after the prescription was written counts as day one (247 CMR 9.04(10)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How many times may Schedule III-V prescription information be transferred for refill purposes, and what single circumstance changes that number?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Once. Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move a never-dispensed electronic Schedule II prescription to another retail pharmacy. Which pathway applies, and does the shared-database allowance help?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The initial-dispensing electronic transfer under 21 CFR 1306.08(e), which reaches Schedules II through V. No: that pathway has no shared-database counterpart and stays one-time, and the prescription must remain electronic and unaltered.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: because Massachusetts requires a pharmacy to transfer on the patient's request, a Schedule IV prescription that has already been transferred once may be transferred again.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 9.14(1) says when a transfer must happen; 21 CFR 1306.25(a) says how many are available, and 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure turn on state law permitting transfers rather than the reverse. Absent a shared real-time, online database, the second transfer is unavailable.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does the federal one-time refill-transfer limit not cap a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer, and what state ceiling applies instead?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because Massachusetts Schedules I-V are the substances the federal schedules list (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a); 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(E)) and Schedule VI holds only prescription drugs in none of them (700.002(F)), so a Schedule VI drug is not a federal Schedule III-V substance and 21 CFR 1306.25 does not reach it. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum remaining refills the prescriber authorized, and 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a refill-authorizing Schedule VI prescription more than one year after issue.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription issued 13 months ago still shows two refills, and the prescriber cannot be reached today. May it be refilled, and what may the pharmacist do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It may not be refilled: under 247 CMR 9.04(12) a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year. Because prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use package.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may execute a prescription transfer, federally and in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Federally, the transfer must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, on both the refill-purpose pathway and the initial-dispensing electronic pathway. Massachusetts adds that a certified pharmacy technician may perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must the transferring and receiving pharmacists record on a refill-purpose transfer of a Schedule III-V prescription, and how long are the records kept?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The transferring pharmacist writes 'VOID' on the prescription (or marks the electronic record as transferred) and records the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the receiving pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name. The receiving pharmacist records the prescription's history (issue date, refills authorized and remaining, dates and locations of earlier fills, and the transferring and originally filling pharmacies), writing 'transfer' on the face of a paper or oral prescription or creating an electronic record for an electronic one. The original and transferred prescriptions are kept for two years from the date of last refill.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How does a Massachusetts pharmacist count days when deciding whether a prescription is within date?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The day after the prescription was written is day one (247 CMR 9.04(10)); the issue date itself is not counted. 247 CMR 9.04(15) disapplies this counting rule at institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

quick_review.text: Federal law bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the issue date and bars more than five refills; only a new prescription lifts either limit.

For pharmacies subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13), a Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after issue, and may not be refilled more than five times; that subsection does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

For pharmacies subject to 247 CMR 9.04(12), a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from issue and may not be refilled after one year, and any refill needs the original prescription to provide for refilling and state the number of refills (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f)).
At a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(10), the day after the prescription was written is day one when deciding whether it is within date.
Massachusetts requires a timely patient-requested transfer, prohibits a transfer fee, and permits a pharmacy to act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer.

Transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information for refill purposes is permitted between pharmacies on a one-time basis only, unless the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database.

Transfer of an unfilled electronic controlled-substance prescription for initial dispensing is a separate federal pathway, permitted between retail pharmacies at the patient's request on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule III or IV refill is requested.
decision_logic.action: Check both elapsed time from issue and the number of prior refills; either exhausted limit blocks the refill.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts Schedule V refill is requested at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13).
decision_logic.action: Apply the five-refill and six-month limits independently.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts Schedule VI refill is requested at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(12).
decision_logic.action: Confirm the original prescription provides for refills and states their number, and that it is within one year of issue. Past one year, or with no refills left, dispense only a professional-judgment supply of up to 14 days or the smallest unit-of-use package, and only if prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in time.

decision_logic.condition: The facility is an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Do not apply the Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13), the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12) or the counting rule in 9.04(10) through those provisions; 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes that facility type.

decision_logic.condition: A patient or authorized agent requests a Massachusetts prescription transfer.
decision_logic.action: Transfer remaining authorized refills timely without charging a transfer fee, subject to the prescription-specific limits.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks to move a Schedule III, IV or V prescription with authorized refills remaining to another pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the prescription has not already been transferred once, unless the two pharmacies electronically share a real-time online database, before applying the Massachusetts transfer duty.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move an ELECTRONIC controlled-substance prescription that has never been dispensed to another retail pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Use the initial-dispensing electronic transfer pathway rather than the refill-transfer rule, keep the prescription in electronic form and unaltered, and treat it as available once only. A never-dispensed paper prescription has no federal transfer pathway.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule III-V prescription is transferred for refill purposes.
decision_logic.action: The transferring pharmacist voids the prescription and records where it went; the receiving pharmacist records the prescription's transfer history, writing 'transfer' on the face of a paper or oral prescription or creating an electronic record for an electronic one; the original and transferred prescriptions are kept for two years from the date of last refill.

ma_vs_federal.text: For Schedule III and IV refills the federal five-refill and six-month limits remain operative when the Massachusetts transfer rules are applied, and so does the separate federal limit permitting a Schedule III-V refill-purpose transfer only once.

Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions and may move up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, with the only ceiling being that a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issue. The federal one-time limit does not cap them, because it reaches only substances in federal Schedules III-V, which Massachusetts places in its own Schedules III-V, while Schedule VI holds prescription drugs included in none of the other schedules.

For Schedule VI the refill limits come from Massachusetts: 247 CMR 9.04(12) makes the prescription valid for one year and bars refills after that, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f) requires the original prescription to provide for and number any refill. The Schedule III-V figures of five refills and six months do not carry across.

A federal controlled-prescription transfer must pass directly between two licensed pharmacists, while Massachusetts lets a certified pharmacy technician do the work for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

exceptions.text: A transfer does not create new refill authority or restart an issue-date clock.
The Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies under 247 CMR 9.04(15).
247 CMR 9.04(15) also removes the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12) and the day-counting rule in 9.04(10) from institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use package; that is not an ordinary refill.
Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization instead of the one-time limit.
The real-time shared-database allowance belongs to the refill-purpose transfer rule; the initial-dispensing electronic transfer carries no such counterpart and stays one-time.

The initial-dispensing transfer in 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is for a prescription's first dispensing. Once a Schedule II prescription has been partially filled, no federal transfer pathway moves its remaining portion to another pharmacy.

timing_deadlines.event: Schedule III-IV refill window
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 6 months after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: No further fill or refill after the federal time limit without practitioner renewal.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts Schedule V refill window at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 6 months after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: No first fill and no refill after the state time limit, and no refill once five are used.

timing_deadlines.event: Refill of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(12)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: No refill after one year; if the prescriber cannot be reached in time, only a professional-judgment supply of up to 14 days or the smallest unit-of-use package.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the one-year point.

timing_deadlines.event: Records of a refill-purpose transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 2 years from the date of last refill
timing_deadlines.consequence: The original and transferred prescriptions must be kept for that period.

timing_deadlines.event: Records of an initial-dispensing electronic transfer
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 2 years from the date of the transfer
timing_deadlines.consequence: Both the transferring and the receiving pharmacy keep the electronic records documenting the transfer for that period.

forms_records.text: On a refill-purpose transfer the transferring pharmacist writes 'VOID' on the face of the invalidated prescription (for an electronic prescription, adds to its record that it has been transferred), records the name, address and DEA registration number of the pharmacy it went to and the name of the receiving pharmacist, and records the date of the transfer and his or her own name.

For a paper prescription, or an oral one reduced to writing, the receiving pharmacist writes 'transfer' on its face, reduces to writing all the information a prescription must contain, and adds the original issue date, the original number of refills authorized, the date of original dispensing, the valid refills remaining with the dates and locations of previous refills, the transferring pharmacy's name, address, DEA registration number and prescription number, the transferring pharmacist's name, and the name, address, DEA registration number and prescription number of the pharmacy that originally filled it. For an electronic prescription transferred electronically, the transferring pharmacist sends that history with the prescription, and the receiving pharmacist creates an electronic record containing it and his or her own name.

The original and transferred prescriptions are kept for two years from the date of last refill, and pharmacies that share one electronic prescription record must still meet every information requirement of a manual transfer.

On an initial-dispensing electronic transfer the transferring pharmacist adds to the electronic record that it has been transferred, the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the receiving pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name; the receiving pharmacist adds 'transfer', the transferring pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the transferring pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name. Software may fill in these fields, but the pharmacist must ensure they are complete and accurate, and both pharmacies keep the records for two years from the date of the transfer.

role_duties.duty: Record the federal transfer data: on a paper or oral prescription, 'transfer' on its face with the full prescription information and transfer history; on an electronic refill transfer, an electronic record with the receiving pharmacist's name and everything transferred; on an initial-dispensing transfer, the entries the electronic-transfer rule lists. The prescription keeps the refills and the issue date it already had.

Transfer the prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay therapy, without charging a fee; on a Schedule III-V refill transfer, the transferring pharmacist writes 'VOID' on the prescription (or marks the electronic record as transferred) and records the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the receiving pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name.
May act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer. This is a permission; the duty to transfer rests on the pharmacy asked to send the prescription.
Communicate a federal controlled-prescription transfer directly between the two of them; the transfer is a pharmacist-to-pharmacist act.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.
Keep the transfer records for two years: from the date of last refill on a refill-purpose transfer, and from the date of transfer, at both pharmacies, on an initial-dispensing electronic transfer.

common_traps.text: Starting a six-month clock at the first dispensing rather than the issue date gives the prescription excess life.
Assuming a transfer renews or expands refill authority confuses movement of a prescription with creation of a new prescription.
Treating the Massachusetts duty to transfer on patient request as removing the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer.
Concluding that a Schedule II prescription can never move between pharmacies overlooks the one-time initial-dispensing transfer of an unfilled electronic prescription.
Letting a certified pharmacy technician transfer a Schedule III-V prescription ignores both the Schedule VI limit on that authority and the federal pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement.
Reading the Massachusetts Schedule V six-month limit as reaching only refills would let a seven-month-old prescription be dispensed for the first time.
Carrying the federal one-time transfer limit across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription refuses a second transfer the regulation allows.
Treating the Schedule VI one-year figure as a transfer bar only lets a prescription be refilled after 247 CMR 9.04(12) has ended its validity.

Sending a partially filled Schedule II prescription through the initial-dispensing transfer overlooks that the pathway is for a prescription's first dispensing, and that no federal pathway moves the remaining portion.

sections.title: Massachusetts Schedule VI
sections.topic: Controlled substance classification
sections.subtopic: Schedule VI prescription lifecycle
learning_objectives: Recognize Schedule VI as the Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule for prescription drugs outside Schedules I through V, rather than as a federal controlled schedule.
Apply Massachusetts prescription elements, oral documentation, electronic-prescribing exceptions, and transfer rules without inventing federal consequences.
Apply the Schedule VI validity clock and the additional-drug consequences instead of treating Schedule VI as a consequence-free label.
Recognise that the Schedule VI classification carries its own scope-of-practice consequence for who may transfer a prescription.
Identify every date gate that can bar a Schedule VI prescription, including the out-of-state 30-day window that sits alongside the one-year validity clock.

orientation.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI is the residual schedule: it holds prescription drugs that Massachusetts has not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V. It is a controlled-substance schedule all the same. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in that chapter, and s. 2(a) establishes the sixth schedule alongside the five that incorporate the federal schedules, so the ordinary prescription drug that carries no federal schedule is, in Massachusetts, a Schedule VI controlled substance. Two consequences follow, and they pull in opposite directions. Schedule VI has no federal counterpart -- 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define Massachusetts Schedules I through V as the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15, and 700.002(F) leaves Schedule VI the prescription drugs outside them -- so Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled, and federal controlled-substance mechanics do not automatically travel with the label. Because Schedule VI is nonetheless a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule, a Massachusetts rule that speaks to controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless that rule carves Schedule VI out: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f), for instance, allows no refill of a controlled-substance prescription unless the original provides for refilling and specifies the number of refills. Reading the label as a synonym for unregulated is the single most productive source of wrong answers in this area.

Every rule taught in this section is Massachusetts law, and it does not all come from one regulator. M.G.L. c. 94C is the statute above both. The Department of Public Health writes 105 CMR 700.000 and 105 CMR 721.000, and from there come the classification itself, the prescription-format scheme, the electronic-prescribing exceptions and the prescription monitoring program. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy writes 247 CMR, and from there come the Schedule VI validity clock, the within-date counting convention and the transfer framework. Some duties are stated twice over. A customer identifier must be presented under the Board's 247 CMR 9.04(14) and, for a pharmacy subject to the monitoring-program reporting requirement, under the Department's 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c)(2) directs the Department to require each pharmacy to collect and report a customer identification number for each monitored prescription. Even inside the Board's own chapter a Schedule VI question can turn on two different one-year rules that sit in two different sections of 247 CMR 9.00 and answer two different questions: 247 CMR 9.04(12) says how long the prescription stays valid, and 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) says how long it stays transferable. Neither restates the other, and a candidate who has collapsed them into one rule will misread whichever question is actually being asked.

On format, Massachusetts starts from a default that every prescription generated in the Commonwealth must be electronic, and then lists the prescriptions excepted from it. The default is statutory and it names Schedule VI: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) provides that a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, and s. 23(g) directs prescribers to issue an electronic prescription for all controlled substances and medical devices. The exception is therefore not a gap the statute left. Section 23(h) directs the commissioner, through regulation, to establish exceptions to s. 17 and s. 23(g) authorizing the limited use of a written and oral prescription where appropriate, and limits them to an enumerated list; Schedule VI is one of the enumerated exceptions the commissioner made, at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9), which is why a Schedule VI prescription may lawfully arrive written or oral. Knowing where the exception comes from matters because it tells you what could move it: the mandate is in the statute, the exception is in a regulation made under s. 23(h), and the six subjects clauses (i) through (vi) name -- veterinarians, temporary technological or electrical failure, a time-limited hardship waiver, emergency situations, prescriptions that cannot be issued electronically under federal or state law, and prescriptions issued outside the jurisdiction of the commonwealth -- do not include Schedule VI, leaving it to the residual clause (vii), under which the commissioner must file a written justification with the house and senate committees on ways and means, the joint committee on public health and the joint committee on mental health, substance use and recovery 90 days before promulgating or amending such a regulation. The exception is narrow in exactly the way candidates tend to forget: it lifts the electronic-format mandate and nothing else. A written Schedule VI prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled. An oral Schedule VI prescription must still be reduced to writing immediately with the information the statute requires. Among the oral-prescription duties, the one Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's later follow-up prescription: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) says in its own terms that its requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, and the follow-up in 105 CMR 721.070(B) is written for oral prescriptions in Schedules II through V. The Failover device points the same way: it is defined as a document that originates as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, so no other schedule can produce one.

A Schedule VI prescription can be stopped by more than one clock, and the exam rewards knowing which clock the facts have started. The general one is the validity limit: a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year. A second one attaches to the prescriber rather than the drug. An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription for filling in Massachusetts, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, and it is that paragraph, not the one-year rule, that makes the out-of-state prescription fillable here in the first place. Both clocks are counted the same way, because in determining whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after the prescription was written as day one. The two clocks fail differently, and the fourteen-day continuation belongs to only one of them: 247 CMR 9.04(12) opens it where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner. Nothing in it reopens the thirty-day authorization in s. 18(c), so an out-of-state prescription past that window is not a candidate for a bridge supply on the strength of the continuation.

Transfer is the other place where the Schedule VI label changes the analysis, and it does so in the pharmacy's direction as well as the patient's. Under 247 CMR 9.14 a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and it may act as the patient's agent to facilitate that transfer. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription, so neither a standing refusal to transfer nor a transfer charge is a matter the pharmacy gets to decide for itself. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III through V prescriptions, carrying up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, subject to the separate one-year transfer bar. Schedule VI is also the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform the transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

Finally, the Schedule VI label is not a promise that no monitoring or identification duty will ever attach. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) has the Department monitor all schedule II to V controlled substances and certain additional drugs, meaning substances the Department determines to carry a bona fide potential for abuse, and 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI so determined. The Commissioner may make that determination for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012, weighing factors such as a risk of addiction, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, or a known contribution to overdose, and on making it notifies all dispensers that they must begin reporting the dispensing of that drug. Once a Schedule VI drug is an additional drug, dispensing it requires a customer identifier from the ultimate user or their agent, subject to the documented-hardship route, under both 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); the Failover route closes, because a Failover does not qualify where the prescription is for an additional drug, and the Department's manual states what the pharmacist does instead: on receiving a Failover for gabapentin, or any other medication designated as an Additional Drug, the pharmacist may not dispense the medication and must contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription; and the dispensing has to be reported on two clocks that apply together. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires the information to be submitted at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, each transmission carrying everything dispensed since the previous one. The operative deadline is whichever of the two arrives first, and across a weekend or a holiday that is always the statute: a Friday dispensing cannot wait for the end of Monday, which the regulation read alone would allow. The label describes the starting point, not the whole of the drug's regulatory position.

comparison_tables.title: What the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes, and what survives it

cells: Where the electronic mandate on a Schedule VI prescription comes from

From the statute, which reaches Schedule VI by name: a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, and prescribers shall issue an electronic prescription for all controlled substances and medical devices. The exception below is a regulation the commissioner was directed to make, not an absence of any statutory duty.
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) and s. 23(g), with the exception power in s. 23(h)
Duty to issue the prescription electronically
No. Schedule VI is an enumerated ePrescribing exception, so the prescription may be issued written or oral.
Statutory prescription elements
Yes. The exception addresses format, not content.
Written-format requirements: signature, plus facsimile transmission or a tamper-resistant form
Yes, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled.
Immediate reduction of an oral prescription to writing with the required information
Yes. The pharmacist's documentation duty is untouched by the exception.
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) and (b)
Practitioner's later follow-up prescription after an oral order
No. The subsection states that its requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
Pharmacist duty to verify that the prescription properly falls within an exception
No such duty is imposed on the receiving pharmacist.

comparison_tables.title: Transfer of a Schedule VI prescription: what 247 CMR 9.14 settles for the pharmacy

cells: May the pharmacy decline the request as a matter of store policy?
No. A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy.
May the pharmacy arrange the transfer on the patient's behalf?
Yes. The pharmacy may act as the patient's agent in order to facilitate a transfer.
May the pharmacy charge for the transfer?
No. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
How many refills move with it?
Up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, Schedule VI transferring in the same manner as Schedules III through V.
Is the prescription too old to transfer?
It is once it is more than one year from the date the prescription was issued.
May a certified pharmacy technician carry it out?
Yes, for Schedule VI only, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient asks Pharmacy B to obtain a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription from Pharmacy A. The prescription was issued ten months ago and has three authorized refills remaining. Pharmacy A says it does not transfer prescriptions as a matter of store policy, and that if it did it would charge the patient a transfer fee first. Pharmacy B has a certified pharmacy technician available and the pharmacist on duty approves the technician's participation.
steps: Classify the drug before anything else. It is not in Massachusetts Schedules I through V, so it is a Schedule VI controlled substance under Massachusetts law, and because no federal schedule lists it the federal transfer mechanics do not reach it.

Check the age of the prescription against the transfer bar rather than the validity clock. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued; ten months is inside that limit.

Test Pharmacy A's policy against 247 CMR 9.14(1). A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, so a standing refusal to transfer cannot stand against the request.
Test the fee against 247 CMR 9.14(3), which provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription. There is no discretion to price the transfer.

Settle what moves. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedules III through V, and may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, so all three remaining refills may travel.

Settle who may act. A certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, and that authority is confined to Schedule VI; do not generalise it to any other schedule.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer proceeds promptly, without a fee, carrying the three remaining refills, and the certified technician may carry it out with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is treating a no-transfer policy and a transfer charge as pharmacy discretion, when 247 CMR 9.14(1) and 9.14(3) remove both; a second error is reaching for a six-month cutoff in place of the one-year transfer limit.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule VI prescription written forty-five days ago by a practitioner licensed and registered in New Hampshire, whose address on the prescription is a New Hampshire office. The patient points out that Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions are good for a year, so the prescription must still be fillable.
steps: Confirm the patient is right about the clock they have named. Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) the prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and forty-five days is well inside that.

Then ask the question the patient has not asked: what makes an out-of-state practitioner's prescription fillable in Massachusetts at all. That authorization is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches prescriptions in Schedules III to VI inclusive.

Read the limit that paragraph attaches to its own grant. It is valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, so it is a second date gate rather than a restatement of the first.
Count the days the way the Board directs, taking the day after the prescription was written as day one. Forty-five days still falls outside the thirty-day window however the count is started.

Do not look for a verification step that will rescue it. The express duty to verify the prescription by telephone or other means runs to Schedules III through V; for a Schedule VI prescription the pharmacist's duty is the general one to determine that the prescription is authentic and valid, and neither duty extends the thirty-day window.

Do not reach for the fourteen-day continuation either. 247 CMR 9.04(12) opens it where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner; this prescription has not expired, and in any event nothing in the continuation reopens the thirty-day authorization in s. 18(c).
worked_examples.resolution: The prescription may not be filled on the out-of-state authorization, because the paragraph that authorizes filling it here reaches only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days. The error the scenario invites is answering from the one-year Schedule VI validity clock alone and never asking where the prescriber wrote from.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient arrives on a Saturday evening out of a maintenance medication. The Schedule VI prescription on file was issued fourteen months ago and shows refills that were never used. A colleague says the prescription has plainly expired, so the fourteen-day continuation is simply what you dispense in that situation.
steps: Establish that the prescription itself is spent. It was valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year, so unused refills on a fourteen-month-old prescription do not survive the expiry.

Read the continuation as the conditional allowance it is. It opens where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills AND the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner; the inability condition governs the expiry branch exactly as it governs the no-refills-remaining branch.

Attempt the authorization first. Try the prescriber, or whoever is covering, and record the attempt. Only once authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner does the professional-judgment allowance become available at all.

If it does open, respect the ceiling. The pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity not to exceed fourteen days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. It is a bridge, not a refill, and it does not renew the expired prescription.

Check the setting before applying any of this. 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), so the validity clock and the continuation attached to it do not reach that facility type.
worked_examples.resolution: Attempt the prescriber before dispensing anything; the fourteen-day continuation becomes available only after that attempt fails to produce timely authorization. The error the colleague makes is reading the expiry branch as self-executing, which drops the inability-to-obtain-authorization condition the regulation attaches to both branches.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts Schedule VI carries two separate one-year rules. State each one and what it measures.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.04(12): a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c): a pharmacy may not transfer a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date the prescription was issued. One measures fillability, the other transferability.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy tells a patient it does not transfer prescriptions, and that in any event it charges for a transfer. Which two provisions dispose of that?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and 247 CMR 9.14(3) provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Besides the one-year validity clock, what second date gate can stop a Schedule VI prescription, and where does it come from?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c): an authorized out-of-state practitioner's prescription in Schedules III to VI inclusive may be filled in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which oral-prescription duty does Schedule VI escape, and which does it keep?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It escapes the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) follow-up prescription, which states that its requirements do not apply to Schedule VI. It keeps the duty to reduce the oral prescription to writing immediately with the information the statute requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception sits at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). What does it not excuse?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It lifts the electronic-format mandate only. The statutory prescription elements still apply, a written prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts excepts Schedule VI from electronic prescribing at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). What does the statute itself say about Schedule VI and electronic prescriptions, and how do the two fit together?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute imposes the mandate and names Schedule VI. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) provides that a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, and s. 23(g) directs prescribers to issue an electronic prescription for all controlled substances and medical devices. Section 23(h) then directs the commissioner, through regulation, to establish exceptions to s. 17 and s. 23(g) authorizing the limited use of a written and oral prescription where appropriate, and limits them to an enumerated list. Schedule VI is not among the six subjects clauses (i) through (vi) name, so it rests on clause (vii), other exceptions as the commissioner determines necessary, which the commissioner may promulgate or amend only after filing a written justification with the house and senate committees on ways and means, the joint committee on public health and the joint committee on mental health, substance use and recovery 90 days beforehand. The Schedule VI exception is a regulatory choice made under a statutory grant, which is why it is found in 105 CMR 721.070(A) and not in the statute.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What turns an ordinary Schedule VI drug into one carrying monitoring and identification duties?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Commissioner's determination under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) that it is an additional drug carrying a bona fide potential for abuse. On that determination dispensers are notified that they must begin reporting it, and a customer identifier is required at dispensing under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3), subject to the documented-hardship route. The reporting then runs on two clocks: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires submission at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, covering everything dispensed since the previous transmission.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile. What is it, and what does it not owe?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Failover. It is considered an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G) hold and the prescription is not for an additional drug.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In deciding whether a prescription is within date, which day is day one?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The day after the prescription was written; the issue date itself is not counted.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name two things 105 CMR 721.020 requires on the face of a prescription that the element list in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) does not.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The quantity of dosage units, under 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3), alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit that the statute requires; and the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional on a prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist who is not authorized for independent practice, under 721.020(E). The refill statement in 721.020(D)(6) is not one of the additions, because s. 22(a) requires it too.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule VI additional drug is dispensed on a Friday afternoon. When must the dispensing reach the Department?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Whichever limit arrives first, because both apply: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires the information to be submitted at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, carrying everything dispensed since the previous transmission. Across the weekend the statute is the stricter, so waiting for the end of Monday is not an option.

quick_review.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.

Every Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), while 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) make Massachusetts Schedules I through V the federal lists, so Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule with no federal counterpart; a Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances, such as the refill condition in s. 23(f), reaches it unless the rule carves Schedule VI out.
Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, while all other validity requirements remain applicable.
An oral controlled-substance prescription must be reduced to writing immediately with the required information; the separate duty to deliver a later follow-up prescription does not reach Schedule VI.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year.

A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug becomes reportable to the prescription monitoring program by a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, and its dispensing requires a customer identifier, subject to the documented-hardship route.

A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and may act as the patient's agent to facilitate the transfer; a standing policy of refusing transfers cannot displace that duty.
A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
Schedule VI is the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform a prescription transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized under 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b); the federal one-time transfer limit in 21 CFR 1306.25(a) reaches prescriptions for substances listed in federal Schedules III, IV and V, so it does not reach a Schedule VI drug that no federal schedule lists.

A prescription written by an authorized out-of-state practitioner is fillable in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive and authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days; that is a second date gate on a Schedule VI prescription, distinct from the one-year validity clock.

Prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing runs on two limits that apply together: at least once every 24 hours under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c), and by the end of the next business day under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5), each transmission covering everything dispensed since the previous one.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I-V.
decision_logic.action: Classify it under Schedule VI, then identify the separate rule governing validity, documentation, dispensing, or transfer.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is written or oral rather than electronic.
decision_logic.action: Do not reject it solely for that format; apply the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception and all remaining prescription requirements, including the form requirements that still govern a written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A patient requests transfer of a Schedule VI prescription with authorized refills remaining.
decision_logic.action: Act on the request rather than declining it: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, 9.14(2) lets the pharmacy act as the patient's agent to facilitate it, and 9.14(3) forbids charging a fee for the transfer. Then apply the Schedule VI mechanics under 247 CMR 9.14(4): the prescription transfers in the same manner as a Schedule III through V prescription and may carry up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, that regulation bars the transfer more than one year after issue, and a certified pharmacy technician may carry it out with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription has expired, being presented more than one year after its issue date, or has no refills remaining, and in either case the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner.
decision_logic.action: Do not refill it. The inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization conditions both branches equally, so attempt the prescriber first in the expired case exactly as in the no-refills-remaining case. Only once that attempt has failed may the pharmacist, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not to exceed 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI medication being dispensed has been designated an additional drug by the Department.
decision_logic.action: Obtain a customer identifier under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3), using the documented hardship route only on its own terms, and treat the dispensing as reportable, submitting at least once every 24 hours under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) and by the end of the next business day under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5).

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI prescription was written by a practitioner licensed and registered outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Apply the out-of-state date gate before the validity clock: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling such a prescription only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days, counting the day after it was written as day one. Determine that the prescription is authentic and valid; note that the express telephone-or-other-means verification requirement runs to Schedules III through V rather than to Schedule VI.

decision_logic.condition: A document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription arrives as a computer-generated facsimile, and the drug on it has been designated an additional drug.
decision_logic.action: Do not dispense on the facsimile, and do not treat the failed condition as something a later prescription can cure. The Department's Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual states that on receiving a Failover for gabapentin, or any other medication designated as an Additional Drug, the pharmacist may not dispense the medication and must instead contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription. The additional-drug condition is the fourth of the conditions a Failover must satisfy, and failing it takes the document outside the Failover route altogether rather than converting it into an oral prescription that owes a follow-up; a Failover that does qualify is dispensed as an oral prescription and needs no additional written follow-up.

ma_vs_federal.text: Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance classification: it makes the drug a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), and it does not itself make the drug federally controlled, because Massachusetts Schedules I through V are the federal lists that Schedule VI sits outside.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug carries Massachusetts prescription-monitoring and customer-identifier duties that the Schedule VI label alone does not imply.

The Massachusetts route for an out-of-state practitioner's prescription is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive; because Schedule VI has no federal counterpart, that thirty-day window is a purely Massachusetts limit and has no federal analogue to be read against it.

exceptions.text: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes that format mandate, not the required prescription elements or oral documentation duties.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may in professional judgment dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), and from 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) as well, so the Board's Schedule VI validity clock, its day-counting convention and its customer-identifier requirement do not reach that facility type. The exclusion reaches only those Board paragraphs: for a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, the Department's own customer-identifier requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3) continues to apply.
In deciding whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after it was written as day one, so the Schedule VI one-year period does not include the issue date itself.

The follow-up duty Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's obligation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) to deliver an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days, or the shorter period federal law requires, where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception under s. 23(h); the parallel follow-up in 105 CMR 721.070(B) is written for oral prescriptions in Schedules II through V and does not reach Schedule VI either.

The Failover is a Schedule VI device: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up, provided its three conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug.

105 CMR 700.012 does not apply to dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital, so neither the monitoring-program reporting duty nor the Department's customer-identifier requirement reaches that dispensing, whatever the drug; 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) otherwise reaches every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses a Schedule II through V controlled substance or an additional drug pursuant to a prescription.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the regulatory one-year limit.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription validity
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 1 year from the date of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: A licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling in Massachusetts a Schedule III through VI prescription issued by an authorized out-of-state practitioner
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Issued within the preceding 30 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within that window, so an older out-of-state Schedule VI prescription is barred even though the one-year validity period has not run.

timing_deadlines.event: Transmission of prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing, under the Department's regulation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: By the end of the next business day
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) also requires each transmission to carry every controlled substance dispensed since the previous one.

timing_deadlines.event: Submission of prescription monitoring information, under the statute
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least once every 24 hours
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) sets this limit alongside the Department's transmission requirement, so a dispensing reported only at the end of the next business day is late whenever more than 24 hours have passed since the pharmacy's previous submission, as after a Friday dispensing held until Monday.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist must immediately reduce an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing with the required Massachusetts prescription information.

A customer identifier must be obtained when dispensing a Schedule VI additional drug, under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and, for a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); the hardship route requires a documented reason and the recipient's printed name and address and signature, with an electronic signature in the case of an electronic prescription.

A written Schedule VI prescription must carry the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) requires a practitioner who dispenses a controlled substance by issuing a written or electronic prescription to state on it the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the date of delivery of the prescription, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the name and address of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any cautionary statements required, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. Read that as the list the statute itself imposes, not as a closed inventory of everything a Massachusetts prescription must carry: the Massachusetts prescription-format regulations reach the same prescription and impose their own requirements alongside the statute.

The format regulation states content the statutory element list does not, and relaxes the patient-identification element in cases the statute does not name: 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires the QUANTITY OF DOSAGE UNITS alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit; (D)(6) repeats the statutory statement indicating the number of times to be refilled; and under (D)(4) the patient's name and address MAY BE LEFT BLANK not only on a veterinary prescription but also on one for naloxone or another Department-approved opioid antagonist and on one issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7), for expedited partner therapy for the treatment of chlamydia, or (A)(12), for a declared public health emergency, for diseases dangerous to public health including sexually transmitted infections, or for any other urgent public health matter.

A prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist must also carry the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional, unless that nurse is authorized for independent practice.

role_duties.duty: Validate required prescription elements even when the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception applies.
Check the Schedule VI validity clock and any additional-drug designation before dispensing rather than treating Schedule VI as consequence-free.
Act on a patient's or agent's transfer request in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and transfer without charging a fee.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as an exemption from all prescription validity requirements is incorrect.
Treating Schedule VI as a federal schedule creates legal consequences that the Massachusetts classification does not supply.

The one-year rule in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) governs transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills and is separate from the one-year prescription validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12); neither should be restated as the other.
Concluding that Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program duties overlooks Schedule VI drugs designated as additional drugs.
Generalising the certified-technician transfer authority beyond Schedule VI ignores the word only in the regulation.
Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as removing every format requirement leaves the pharmacist filling a written prescription that no permitted format supports.

Treating a refusal to transfer, or a charge for transferring, as a matter of pharmacy discretion overlooks the affirmative timely-transfer duty in 247 CMR 9.14(1) and the fee prohibition in 247 CMR 9.14(3).

Treating the one-year validity clock as the only date gate on a Schedule VI prescription misses the separate thirty-day limit M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) places on an out-of-state practitioner's Schedule III through VI prescription.

Reciting the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) elements as the complete set of content and exception rules for a Massachusetts prescription treats a statutory list as exhaustive, when the prescription-format regulations govern the same prescription in their own right.

Naming the veterinary prescription as the only case where the patient's name and address may be left blank misses the naloxone and opioid-antagonist limb and the two ePrescribing-exception limbs in 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).

Reading Schedule VI as a label outside controlled-substance law misses M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), which make a Schedule VI drug a Massachusetts controlled substance, and with it every Massachusetts controlled-substance rule that does not carve Schedule VI out.

Teaching the monitoring deadline as the end of the next business day alone drops the statutory limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c), which requires submission at least once every 24 hours and is the stricter of the two across a weekend or holiday.

Reading the 247 CMR 9.04(15) exclusion as ending the customer-identifier duty for an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy overlooks the Department's separate requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3).

Reading 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) as proof that the electronic-prescribing mandate never reached Schedule VI inverts the scheme: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) names Schedule VI in the mandate itself, and the exception exists because s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish exceptions by regulation.

Dispensing a Failover for an additional drug and waiting for a follow-up prescription gets the consequence backwards twice over: the pharmacist may not dispense that Failover at all and must contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription, while a Failover that does qualify is dispensed and owes no follow-up.

sections.title: Federal and Massachusetts Rule Interaction
sections.topic: Federal and state interaction
sections.subtopic: Layered controlled-prescription analysis
learning_objectives: Solve a federal-state interaction by identifying the same actor, event, and prescription pathway under both sources.
Avoid selecting a familiar federal limit before checking Massachusetts conditions that also govern the transaction.

orientation.text: Two sovereigns reach the same dispensing at the same instant, and neither one announces where the other stops mattering. Federal controlled-substance regulation mostly draws an outer boundary: it describes the most a registrant may do without violating federal law, and it does not confer authority to do that thing where the pharmacy actually stands. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) says so in its own text. A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at a patient's or practitioner's request only if all four of its conditions are met: the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, the federal regulations and State law; the request comes from the patient, a parent or legal guardian of a minor patient, a caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney, or the practitioner who wrote the prescription; and the total dispensed across all partial fillings does not exceed the total prescribed. Two of the four point at the state. Read the first exactly: it asks for an absence of state prohibition, not for affirmative state permission, so a jurisdiction that says nothing does not block the partial fill. The second reaches further than it looks, because a prescription that falls short of what State law requires of it has not been written in accordance with State law, and the federal permission is unavailable until that defect is cured.

Now put one patient-requested Schedule II partial fill in front of both sources and take it part by part, because the relationship changes from part to part. Whether the pharmacist dispenses the lesser quantity is a state duty inside a federal permission: federal law permits the partial fill, while under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist SHALL dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it. Where the remaining portion may be dispensed is the same answer under both sovereigns: s. 18(d3/4) allows only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity to dispense it, and federal law gives a second pharmacy no route either, because 21 CFR 1306.08(e) transfers an electronic prescription only for its initial dispensing, 21 CFR 1306.25 moves only Schedule III-V prescription information for refills, and DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits a partially filled prescription to be transferred for its remaining portion. What record the dispensing leaves is cumulative: the pharmacist notes that the patient requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed, and the pharmacy keeps a federal dispensing record for each partial filling, while Massachusetts separately requires a notation of the partial fill and the quantity in the patient's record, accessible to the prescriber on request. Neither record stands in for the other. By when the remaining portion must go out has two matching answers: not later than 30 days after the prescription was written, or 72 hours after issue for an emergency oral prescription, federally, and not later than 30 days after the issue date in Massachusetts.

Other parts of the same transaction are governed by Massachusetts alone. The federal remainder clock in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) times only the remaining portions of a requested partial fill; it does not time the first dispensing. Massachusetts does: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance, so the first dispensing of an in-state prescription, partial or full, has to fall within those 30 days, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs. Section 18(d3/4) adds a shorter limit on the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), the two out-of-state routes: not more than 5 days after the issue date. 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same five-day limit, counted in calendar days, wherever the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth. And M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) requires any prescription a practitioner issues for an opioid substance in Schedule II to include a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with s. 18(d3/4), in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. That duty falls on the prescriber as a matter of what the prescription must contain. It is a different duty from the patient-record notation made at each partial dispensing, and running the two together puts the obligation on the wrong actor. Silence on the federal side is not an argument that any of these points is unregulated.

A different interaction is harder to see, because nothing about it looks like a conflict. Federal law and Massachusetts law each carry a five-refill limit and a six-month limit measured from the issue date, and the two numbers are identical. The scopes are not. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is addressed to a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV: no such prescription may be filled or refilled more than six months after the date it was issued, and none authorised to be refilled may be refilled more than five times. 247 CMR 9.04(13) states the same two limits for Schedule V, and for Schedule V alone. Massachusetts then narrows its own provision by facility rather than by schedule: 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. Storing 'five refills, six months' as a single remembered fact loses all of this. The figure is correct in two places and controlling in neither until the schedule -- and, in Massachusetts, the facility -- is matched to the transaction in front of you.

The working method that survives all of these patterns is the same one. Fix the schedule, the actor, the triggering event, the pathway and the facility before opening any rule. Then take each part of the transaction in turn -- whether it may happen, who must do it, where, by when, and what record it leaves -- and apply every rule, from either sovereign, whose scope actually reaches that part. A federal figure that answers one part, as the 30-day remainder clock answers by when, says nothing about another part, such as where the remainder may be dispensed. Finally, read the stem for which sovereign it is asking about: a stem that names a place rather than a body of law is asking about both.
