worked_examples.scenario: A New Hampshire physician's written prescription for amphetamine salts, a nonnarcotic Schedule II substance, is presented at your Massachusetts pharmacy three days after it was issued. The prescriber is registered in New Hampshire and under federal law. Your technician says verification is only needed for Schedules III through V. What do you do?
steps: Identify the pathway. A nonnarcotic Schedule II from an out-of-state practitioner is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d), not s. 18(c) and not the narcotic route in s. 18(d1/2).

Check the issuing conditions the subsection states: licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, registered in another state where the practitioner resides or practices if that state requires it, and registered under federal law to write prescriptions. The facts give you both registrations.

Check the window against the fill rather than the counter. s. 18(d) authorizes the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days; at three days, counting the day after it was written as day one, a fill today is inside it.

Apply the duty the pathway states. s. 18(d) requires the filling pharmacist both to determine authenticity and validity in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment and to verify the prescription by telephone or other means. The technician is wrong: verification is not a Schedule III through V speciality.
If verification cannot be obtained, do not fill. Document the good faith efforts; the statute protects a pharmacist who refuses on that basis.
After filling, start the post-fill clock: a copy goes to the Department within 30 days of the filling, without the patient's name and address.
worked_examples.resolution: Verify before filling. Skipping verification here would fill a Schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill, and the Department copy is still owed 30 days after the filling.

worked_examples.scenario: A Connecticut nurse practitioner's prescription for a Schedule VI antihypertensive is presented 20 days after issue. Your colleague wants to telephone the prescriber's office to verify before filling, and is frustrated that nobody is answering after hours. Must the fill wait for that call?
steps: Identify the pathway. Schedule VI from an out-of-state practitioner falls under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches schedules III to VI inclusive and asks that the practitioner be duly licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, duly registered in the state wherein the practitioner resides if that state requires it, and duly registered under federal law.
Check the window. s. 18(c) authorizes filling a prescription issued within the preceding 30 days; at 20 days, counting the day after it was written as day one, a fill today is inside it.

Read the duty precisely. s. 18(c) imposes the authenticity-and-validity determination on every prescription it reaches, but conditions telephone or other verification on the substance being in schedules III to V. Schedule VI is outside that condition.

So the pharmacist still has to be satisfied, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid -- but the separate telephone-verification duty is not triggered.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The fill does not wait on a verification call that this pathway does not require. Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the telephone-verification duty, and this is the distinction the wording of s. 18(c) turns on.

worked_examples.scenario: A Rhode Island physician's oxycodone prescription, a Schedule II narcotic, is presented four days after issue. The patient asks for only part of the quantity today. Which five-day rule are you applying, and what closes when?
steps: Identify the pathway. A narcotic Schedule II from a contiguous state is s. 18(d1/2), and Rhode Island is contiguous with the commonwealth.

The first five-day rule is the filling window: s. 18(d1/2) applies only to authorizations for the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, so it governs whether anything may be dispensed on this prescription today. At four days it does.
Verify the prescription by telephone or other means, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.

The second five-day rule is the partial-fill limit, and it is a different rule with a different source. s. 18(d3/4) requires the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or (d1/2) to be filled not more than five days after the issue date, and 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same limit as a presentation deadline of five calendar days where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth. Both point at today's dispensing; what the partial-fill rule adds is what happens next.
Follow the remainder to its own clock: it may be filled not later than 30 days after the issue date, and only by this pharmacy, which is the clock that outlives the five-day window.
worked_examples.resolution: Both five-day rules are satisfied today, and they are not the same rule: one decides whether the out-of-state subsection authorizes a fill at all, the other governs the initial partial dispensing and carries the 30-day remainder clock. Note the partial dispensing and the quantity in the patient record, keep any remainder at this pharmacy, complete it within 30 days of the issue date, and send the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of the filling.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives by commercial carrier a written prescription for a narcotic Schedule II substance, written by a practitioner licensed and registered in Pennsylvania and registered under federal law, for a patient who lives in Pennsylvania, to be shipped to the patient's home there. A colleague says Massachusetts allows narcotic Schedule II fills only on prescriptions from Maine or a contiguous state, so this one must be refused.
steps: Identify where in s. 18(d1/2) these facts sit. The subsection's first paragraph is about who may issue a narcotic Schedule II prescription for filling here; a later paragraph of the same subsection provides that nothing in it prohibits a retail pharmacy operating within the commonwealth from filling such prescriptions for residents of states other than Maine and the contiguous states.

Work through that paragraph's conditions instead of assuming them. The pharmacy must be licensed for retail by the commonwealth and, if applicable, registered with the appropriate regulatory authorities in the state from which the prescription is received and with the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the prescription must be filled by a pharmacist licensed and registered in the originating state where that state requires it.

Check the prescriber against the state of delivery rather than against Massachusetts. The writer must be licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state to which the prescription is to be delivered, and registered under federal law; an authorized nurse practitioner or physician assistant qualifies on the same terms.

Check how the prescription arrived and how the drug will leave. It must be received by mail, commercial carrier or an equivalent electronic means authorized by federal law, and the substance must be delivered by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, without entering the hands of anyone in the commonwealth outside the postal service or the carrier selected.

Apply the duties the paragraph attaches to the fill itself: determine that the prescription is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state it came from, verify it by telephonic or other means, do not fill it if verification cannot be obtained, comply in full with the laws and regulations of the state the patient lives in on the issuance and filling of prescriptions, since that is the state the delivery reaches, and meet that same state's reporting requirements, including enrolment in and adherence to its prescription monitoring program where that applies.
worked_examples.resolution: The colleague has read the first paragraph of s. 18(d1/2) and stopped. A Massachusetts retail pharmacy may fill this prescription and ship it, provided every condition the later paragraph states is met, and the reason to refuse would be a failed verification or an unmet condition rather than the prescriber's state. The conditions to work are the ones that paragraph states, including the delivery state's own law on the issuance and filling of prescriptions; and the paragraph does not turn the pharmacy into a mail order pharmacy, which the section says nothing in it authorizes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which out-of-state pathway carries the authenticity duty but NOT the telephone-verification duty, and why?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedule VI under s. 18(c). The subsection reaches schedules III to VI but conditions verification on the substance being in schedules III to V.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Out-of-state filling windows: schedules III through VI, ______ days; either schedule II route, ______ days. What date must fall inside the window?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30; 5. Each subsection authorizes the FILLING of prescriptions issued within the preceding window, so the fill must happen while the prescription is still that young; a prescription presented in time but filled later is outside the authorization.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: verification by telephone or other means is required only for out-of-state schedule III through V prescriptions.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) each state the verification duty independently for the nonnarcotic and narcotic schedule II routes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under the first paragraph of s. 18(d1/2), where must the practitioner be registered, and what do the later paragraphs of that subsection add?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Maine, or a state contiguous with the commonwealth. Two later paragraphs provide that nothing in the subsection prohibits a retail pharmacy operating here from filling narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of other states, delivered by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, or for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered directly to the facility by a courier the pharmacy employs or contracts -- each on the conditions its own paragraph states.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name three conditions the s. 18(d1/2) paragraph attaches to filling a narcotic schedule II prescription for a resident of another state.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any three of: Massachusetts retail licensure plus registration with the origin state's regulatory authorities and the Drug Enforcement Administration as applicable; a filling pharmacist licensed and registered in the originating state where it requires that; a prescriber licensed and registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state of delivery and registered under federal law; receipt by mail, commercial carrier or an equivalent federally authorized electronic means; a determination that the prescription is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state it came from, with verification; compliance with the delivery state's prescription laws and reporting requirements, including its monitoring program; and delivery by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacist refuses an out-of-state prescription because verification could not be obtained. What protects them, and what is the condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute provides they shall not be held liable for the refusal, provided documented good faith efforts were made to determine authenticity and validity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Department copy after filling an out-of-state Schedule II prescription is due within ______, measured from ______, and must omit ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30 days; the filling; the patient's name and address.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the two distinct five-day rules in this area, and say what each one decides.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The filling window in s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2), which decides whether the subsection authorizes filling the prescription here at all; and the initial partial-dispensing limit in s. 18(d3/4), implemented by 105 CMR 721.055(A), which governs the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled under those subsections and carries the 30-day remainder clock with it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In deciding whether a prescription is within date, which day is day one, and how does 105 CMR 721.055(A) count?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.04(10): the day after the prescription was written is day one, so the issue date itself is not counted. 105 CMR 721.055(A) runs five CALENDAR days from the prescription issue date, and attaches that limit where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does s. 18(c) require of the issuing practitioner, in its own words, and how does that differ from s. 18(d)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That the practitioner be duly licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, duly registered in the state wherein he resides, if required, and duly registered under federal law to write prescriptions. Section 18(d) instead speaks of registration in another state where the practitioner resides or practices, if required, and likewise requires federal registration.

quick_review.text: An authorized out-of-state practitioner's schedule III through VI prescription is fillable in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding 30 days.
Either out-of-state schedule II route authorizes filling only a prescription issued within the preceding five days, under separate subsections with their own issuing conditions.

All three subsections require the issuing practitioner to be registered under federal law to write prescriptions; s. 18(c) asks for registration in the state wherein the practitioner resides, if required, while s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) ask for the state where the practitioner resides or practices.
The first paragraph of the schedule II narcotic route reaches a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

Later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) let a retail pharmacy operating here fill narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of other states, delivered by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, and for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered by the pharmacy's own courier, each on its stated conditions.

Every out-of-state pathway requires the filling pharmacist to determine authenticity and validity; telephone verification is additionally required on schedules III through V and on both schedule II routes, leaving schedule VI as the one pathway without it.

Where the out-of-state prescription is oral and in schedules III through V, the pharmacist records having requested that the practitioner deliver or mail a written prescription to the dispensing pharmacy within seven days or the shorter period federal law requires.

A prescription filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) has its own five-day limit on the INITIAL PARTIAL DISPENSING, separate from the window that authorizes the fill, and the remaining portion runs to 30 days after the issue date at the same pharmacy.

105 CMR 721.055(A) states the initial partial-fill limit as five calendar days from the prescription issue date and triggers it off the prescriber's address on the prescription being outside the Commonwealth.
In determining whether a prescription is within date, 247 CMR 9.04(10) counts the day after the prescription was written as day one.
After filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription the pharmacist delivers a copy to the Department within 30 days, with the patient's name and address removed.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state practitioner's prescription is presented.
decision_logic.action: Identify the subsection first: schedules III through VI run on s. 18(c) and 30 days, a nonnarcotic schedule II on s. 18(d) and five days, a narcotic schedule II on s. 18(d1/2), five days and a narrower list of issuing states. Check the issuing condition that subsection states, federal registration included.

decision_logic.condition: You have identified the pathway and are deciding whether the window is open.
decision_logic.action: Measure to the fill, not to the presentation: the subsection authorizes filling a prescription issued within the preceding 30 or five days, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is inside the window of its pathway.
decision_logic.action: Determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid. Then verify by telephone or other means unless the substance is schedule VI, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.

decision_logic.condition: Verification cannot be obtained.
decision_logic.action: Refuse the fill and document the good faith efforts made; the statute protects the refusal on that basis.

decision_logic.condition: The out-of-state schedule III-V prescription was communicated orally.
decision_logic.action: Record that you requested the practitioner deliver or mail the written prescription to the dispensing pharmacy within seven days or the shorter period federal law requires; the period runs on the practitioner's delivery.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) is partially dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Fill the initial partial dispensing not more than five days after the issue date, treating 105 CMR 721.055(A) as five calendar days from that date where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth; note the partial fill and quantity in the patient record; keep any remainder at this pharmacy and fill it not later than 30 days after the issue date.

decision_logic.condition: A narcotic schedule II prescription is to be filled here for a resident of another state, or for a patient in a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state.
decision_logic.action: Work the conditions of the applicable later paragraph of s. 18(d1/2): Massachusetts retail licensure and the registrations it names; for the other-state paragraph, a prescriber registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state of delivery, receipt by mail, carrier or an equivalent federally authorized electronic means, authenticity, validity, legitimacy and legality in the originating state with verification, compliance with the delivery state's prescription and reporting law, and delivery by mail or carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence; for the long-term care paragraph, delivery directly to the facility by the pharmacy's employed or contracted courier.

decision_logic.condition: You have filled an out-of-state schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the filling, excluding the patient's name and address.

ma_vs_federal.text: The federal six-month schedule III and IV clock does not license an out-of-state prescription that no Massachusetts paragraph authorizes filling; the Massachusetts window is the gate that closes first.
The out-of-state oral schedule III through V follow-up period is stated as seven days or the shorter period federal law requires, so a shorter federal period governs where one exists.

The s. 18(d1/2) paragraph for residents of other states does not displace the delivery state's law: it conditions the fill on full compliance with that state's laws and regulations on the issuance and filling of prescriptions and on its reporting requirements, including its prescription monitoring program where applicable.

exceptions.text: The five-day schedule II window sits in separate subsections that also carry their own conditions on which issuing states qualify, so it is not simply a shorter version of the same rule.

These subsections matter where the prescriber is not registered under chapter 94C: a practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered under the chapter issues under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a), and the five-day filling window in s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) does not govern that prescription.

Later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) provide that nothing in the subsection prohibits a retail pharmacy operating within the commonwealth from filling narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of states other than Maine and the contiguous states, on six stated conditions ending in mail or commercial-carrier delivery to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, or for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered directly to the facility by a courier the pharmacy employs or contracts.
Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the separate telephone-verification duty.

The out-of-state schedule II subsections authorize the filling only. They do not authorize the practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances as provided in section 9 or to practise within the commonwealth, and the section states that nothing in it authorizes a mail order pharmacy -- which is the backdrop to the later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2), where it is a Massachusetts retail pharmacy that fills and ships.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling an out-of-state schedule III through VI prescription under s. 18(c)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The prescription must have been issued within the preceding 30 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: Outside the window this pathway does not authorize the fill at all.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The prescription must have been issued within the preceding 5 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: The 30-day figure does not carry across to schedule II, and the limit reaches a full fill as well as an initial partial fill.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial partial dispensing of a schedule II prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or (d1/2)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 5 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same limit as presentation for initial partial fill within five calendar days, where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining portion of that partially dispensed prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remainder closes on the issue-date clock and only at the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner delivery of an out-of-state oral schedule III-V written follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days or the shorter period federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period governs the practitioner's delivery; what the pharmacist owes is the record that the request was made.

timing_deadlines.event: Department copy after filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 30 days after the filling
timing_deadlines.consequence: This clock runs from the filling, unlike the filling windows and the partial-fill limits in this section, which run from the prescription issue date.

forms_records.text: On the out-of-state oral schedule III-V pathway the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.

An initial partial dispensing and any later dispensing of the remaining portion carry the s. 18(d3/4) patient-record notation of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed, accessible to the prescriber on request; 105 CMR 721.055(C) states the same duty for the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee.
The Department copy excludes the patient's name and address, and neither the copy nor its contents is a public record.
Where verification cannot be obtained, the good faith efforts made are themselves the record that protects the refusal.

A pharmacy filling under the s. 18(d1/2) paragraph for residents of other states must comply with the delivery state's reporting requirements, including enrolment in and adherence to that state's prescription monitoring program or an equivalent program, where applicable.

role_duties.duty: Determine authenticity and validity on every out-of-state pathway, and verify by telephone or other means on every pathway except schedule VI.
Refuse to fill an out-of-state prescription for which verification cannot be obtained.
Measure each window to the fill, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one.
Deliver the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription.

role_duties.role: Retail pharmacy filling under the s. 18(d1/2) delivery paragraphs
role_duties.duty: Hold Massachusetts retail licensure and the registrations the paragraph names, and deliver only as it permits: by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, or directly to a long-term care facility by a courier the pharmacy employs or contracts.

common_traps.text: Treating verification as a schedule III through V feature fills an out-of-state nonnarcotic schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill.
Carrying the 30-day out-of-state window to a schedule II prescription accepts one that Massachusetts authorizes filling only within five days of issue.

Reading the window as a deadline for presenting the prescription lets a pharmacist accept it in time and fill it out of time; the subsections authorize the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding window.
Filling an out-of-state schedule III-V prescription on the federal six-month clock skips both the Massachusetts window and the verification gate.

Treating the seven-day follow-up period as the pharmacist's deadline reverses the timed event: the period runs on the practitioner's delivery of the written prescription, and the pharmacist's duty is to record the request.

Reading the five-day figure as one rule merges the window that authorizes the fill with the separate limit on an initial partial dispensing, and loses the 30-day remainder clock that only the second carries.
Counting the initial partial-fill limit in business days, or from something other than the prescription issue date, misses that 105 CMR 721.055(A) counts five calendar days from that date.
Measuring the Department copy's 30 days from the issue date rather than from the filling misses that this is the one duty here keyed to the dispensing event.
Demanding a verification call on a schedule VI out-of-state prescription applies a duty s. 18(c) conditions on schedules III to V.

Refusing a narcotic schedule II prescription for a resident of another state because the prescriber is outside Maine and the contiguous states stops at the first paragraph of s. 18(d1/2) and misses the later paragraph that permits the fill on stated conditions.

learning_objectives: Apply each sovereign's definition of an emergency situation, and notice that they are not the same test.

Trace why a Massachusetts emergency oral prescription runs on the ePrescribing-exception route rather than the two-day electronic clause, and how the regulation's seven business days sit beside the statute's 7 days.
Identify which follow-up period actually binds when both sovereigns reach the same prescription.
State what the pharmacist must write down, attach or annotate at each stage.
Name the consequence the regulation attaches to the pharmacist's own failure to notify the DEA.

orientation.text: Schedule II normally means a signed prescription before the drug leaves the shelf: 21 CFR 1306.11(a) lets a pharmacist dispense a Schedule II drug only pursuant to a written prescription signed by the practitioner, except as paragraph (d) provides. The emergency oral pathway is that exception, and it is built in three layers. The first is a gate, and each sovereign defines it differently. Federal law, in 21 CFR 290.10, requires the prescribing practitioner to determine that immediate administration is necessary, that no appropriate alternative treatment is available including a drug that is not in Schedule II, and that it is not reasonably possible to provide a WRITTEN prescription before the dispensing. Massachusetts, in 105 CMR 721.010, asks whether immediate administration of the controlled substance is necessary and then either that it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an ELECTRONIC prescription before the dispensing or that the practitioner determines the electronic requirement would cause a delay adversely impacting the patient; it also takes in any other Emergency Situation the Commissioner defines in Department guidance. Massachusetts carries no no-alternative-treatment element at all.

On Massachusetts facts the two definitions are cumulative, because each sovereign conditions its own permission on its own test: 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens the oral route only in an emergency situation as 290.10 defines it, and 105 CMR 721.060(B) lets a pharmacist dispense a Schedule II substance on the prescriber's authorization only in case of an Emergency Situation as 721.010 defines it. Facts that satisfy the Massachusetts definition but not the federal one leave the oral route closed: an appropriate non-Schedule II alternative defeats federal element (b), and a signed written prescription that could reach the pharmacy before the dispensing defeats element (c) even where an electronic prescription cannot be transmitted. The three federal elements are the prescribing practitioner's determination; the Massachusetts definition is written around the prescriber's circumstances and makes its delay limb the practitioner's determination. 105 CMR 721.070(C) spares a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid oral prescription from verifying that it properly falls under an ePrescribing exception, which is a question of Massachusetts exception status and does not supply a federal element the facts defeat.

Once both gates are passed the pharmacist may dispense on the oral authorization, but only the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, and, where the prescriber is not known to the pharmacist, only after a reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered individual practitioner, which Massachusetts states as a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization was issued by a prescribing practitioner. The prescription is immediately reduced to writing with everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature, and on Massachusetts facts with everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires, 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) allowing it to be entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead of written out. Those Massachusetts duties are the statute's own, and s. 20 states them for any oral controlled-substance prescription rather than for the emergency alone. Section 20(a) directs the pharmacist, upon receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance from an authorized practitioner, to reduce it to writing immediately on a prescription form and to record an enumerated list of particulars, and s. 20(b) states the authentication duty separately: if the prescribing practitioner is not known to the pharmacist, the pharmacist shall make a reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered practitioner. The emergency regulation restates neither list. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) sends the record back to s. 20(a), and 721.060(B)(3) puts the good faith effort in its own words, so what the writing has to contain is fixed by the statute and not by the emergency paragraph. Massachusetts is explicit about what the emergency does and does not touch: 105 CMR 721.060(A) waives the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, and the written and oral prescriptions it then permits must comply with all other prescription requirements.

The third layer is the follow-up, and it is where candidates lose the question. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) opens with an ELECTRONIC follow-up within 2 days whenever a practitioner prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription, which is tempting to read as the stricter Massachusetts answer. That clause is the statute's rule for a practitioner who has received no exception from using an electronic prescription from the commissioner under s. 23(h); the same subsection sends a practitioner who has received one to a WRITTEN prescription within not more than 7 days, or such shorter period as federal law requires. Section 23(h) is where those exceptions come from: it directs the commissioner to establish them through regulation and limits them to a list that includes emergency situations, 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations accordingly, and 105 CMR 721.020(A) makes a 721.070 exception the only basis for a non-electronic prescription generated in the Commonwealth. A lawful Massachusetts emergency oral prescription is therefore always issued under an exception, and the 2-day clause is not the route it travels.

Where that leaves the count is worth stating plainly, because the Massachusetts texts do not use the same unit. The statute's exception route is not more than 7 days for a written follow-up. 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the emergency prescription to 105 CMR 721.070(B), which gives not more than seven business days for a written or electronic one, or such shorter period as federal law requires; 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states seven business days directly for this pathway; and the Department's manual states seven business days for every oral schedule II through V prescription issued under an exception, the emergency included. The statute keys its 7-day route to a practitioner who has RECEIVED an exception, a phrase that fits the applied-for waiver most naturally and that the statute does not confine to waiver holders, so the emergency oral prescription reads onto the 7-day route while the regulation and the Department measure it in seven business days. For this prescription the difference changes nothing: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription, 721.070(B) yields in its own words to that shorter federal period, and seven days run out before seven business days do. Seven days from the oral authorization is the deadline that satisfies every period these texts state.

The record layer finishes the pathway. The prescriber writes on the face of the follow-up the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order, both of which 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires and the first of which 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) requires as well; on Massachusetts facts the follow-up also indicates that it is issued to document an oral prescription, which M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires of an electronic or written follow-up, 105 CMR 721.070(B) requires of a written one, and the Department's manual states for every emergency follow-up. The pharmacist attaches a paper follow-up to the writing made on the telephone and annotates the record of an electronic one with the original authorization and the date of the oral order. If no complying follow-up is delivered, the pharmacist notifies the nearest DEA office, and the pharmacist's own failure to notify voids the federal authority to have dispensed without a written prescription.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts prescriber telephones at 7pm on a Friday from home. A patient needs morphine oral solution tonight; the prescriber tells you that no drug outside Schedule II would be an appropriate treatment, that the practice's e-prescribing system is down, and that there is no way to get a signed paper prescription to your pharmacy before the dose is needed. The prescriber is not known to you. How much may you dispense, and by when must the follow-up arrive?
steps: Work the federal gate first, because federal law opens no other oral route for a Schedule II drug. 21 CFR 290.10 needs all three of the prescriber's determinations: immediate administration is necessary, no appropriate alternative treatment is available including a drug outside Schedule II, and a written prescription cannot reasonably be provided before the dispensing. An e-prescribing outage on its own would not establish the third element; here the prescriber has also ruled out getting a signed paper prescription to you in time.

Work the Massachusetts gate. Immediate administration is necessary and it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an electronic prescription before the dispensing, so this is an Emergency Situation under 105 CMR 721.010. Both definitions are satisfied, and on Massachusetts facts both must be.
Because the prescriber is not known to you, make a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered prescribing practitioner before dispensing anything.

Limit the quantity to what is adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period. Anything beyond the emergency period needs a paper or electronic prescription signed by the practitioner, not this authorization.
Immediately reduce the oral prescription to writing, carrying every required element except the practitioner's signature.

Now pick the follow-up clock. The emergency is an enumerated ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), one of those M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish, so the 2-day electronic clause that opens s. 20(c) is not the route. The statute's exception route states not more than 7 days; 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 721.070(B) for not more than seven business days or such shorter period as federal law requires; and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states seven business days for this pathway directly.

Supply the federal period. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription. That matches the statute's 7 days and runs out before seven business days, so seven days from the oral authorization is the deadline every text accepts.
worked_examples.resolution: Dispense only the emergency-period quantity, after the reasonable good faith effort to identify the prescriber, reduce the order to writing immediately, and expect the follow-up within seven days of the oral authorization bearing Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, the date of the oral order, and the indication that it documents an oral prescription. Answering two days applies the statute's no-exception clause to a prescription issued under an exception; answering seven business days overlooks the shorter federal period that 721.070(B) defers to in its own words.

worked_examples.scenario: Eight days have passed since you dispensed on an emergency oral Schedule II authorization. You have telephoned the prescriber's office twice and documented both calls, and no written or electronic follow-up has arrived. A colleague says the documented calls discharge your duty. Is that right?
steps: The practitioner's 7-day federal period has expired, so the follow-up is missing rather than merely late.

Federal law places a duty on you at that point: notify the nearest office of the DEA that the practitioner failed to deliver the follow-up prescription. Chasing the prescriber is not the duty the regulation names, and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(5) places a matching duty on the pharmacist where the practitioner fails to deliver in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4).
Read the consequence attached to your own omission. Failure of the pharmacist to notify voids the authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to dispense without a written prescription.
worked_examples.resolution: The colleague is wrong. Documented calls do not substitute for the notification, and the consequence of skipping it falls on the dispensing itself: it loses the federal authority it rested on.

worked_examples.scenario: On a Wednesday afternoon a Massachusetts practice's e-prescribing system goes down. A prescriber telephones an oral order for a Schedule II opioid for a patient who needs a dose within the hour, and mentions that the patient's daughter is at the practice and could bring a signed paper prescription to your pharmacy in twenty minutes. Your technician says the outage makes this a Massachusetts Emergency Situation, so the telephone order can be dispensed. Is that right?
steps: Test the Massachusetts definition. Immediate administration is necessary and it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an electronic prescription before the dispensing, so the facts fit the Emergency Situation in 105 CMR 721.010.

Test the federal definition separately. 21 CFR 290.10(c) asks whether it is not reasonably possible to provide a WRITTEN prescription to be presented before the dispensing. A signed paper prescription can be in your hands within the hour, so that element fails, and 290.10(b) would have to be satisfied as well.

Draw the consequence. Without a federal emergency situation the oral route in 21 CFR 1306.11(d) is closed and 1306.11(a) requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner; the Massachusetts permission in 105 CMR 721.060(B) is state law and supplies no federal element.

Take the signed paper prescription when it arrives. Massachusetts permits a written prescription where electronic prescribing is unavailable because of a temporary technological or electrical failure, and 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to carry the practitioner's signature and, since it is handed over rather than transmitted by facsimile, to be written on a tamper-resistant form.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The facts satisfy the Massachusetts definition but not the federal one, and on Massachusetts facts the oral Schedule II route needs both. The error the scenario invites is treating an electronic-prescribing outage as settling the federal question, which asks about a written prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Federal law adds one element to the emergency-situation test that Massachusetts does not state at all. Name it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: That no appropriate alternative treatment is available, including administration of a drug which is not a Schedule II controlled substance (21 CFR 290.10(b)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The federal emergency test turns on the impracticability of providing a ______ prescription; the Massachusetts test turns on the impracticability of generating or transmitting an ______ prescription.
retrieval_prompts.answer: written; electronic.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescriber's facts satisfy 105 CMR 721.010 but not 21 CFR 290.10. May the pharmacist dispense the Schedule II drug on the oral authorization?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens the oral route only in a federal emergency situation, and 1306.11(a) otherwise requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner; the Massachusetts permission in 105 CMR 721.060(B) does not supply the missing federal element.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does the 2-day electronic follow-up that opens M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) NOT govern a Massachusetts emergency oral Schedule II prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because that clause is the statute's rule for a practitioner who has received no exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), and emergency situations are among the exceptions s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates; the statute's exception route states not more than 7 days, and 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 721.070(B).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 105 CMR 721.070(B) states the follow-up as not more than seven business days, or ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: such shorter period as is required by federal law, which here is the 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4), counted from the practitioner's authorization of the emergency oral prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Federal law requires two things on the face of the follow-up prescription, and Massachusetts adds a third. Name all three.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order (21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4); the first is required by 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) as well), plus the indication that the prescription is issued to document an oral prescription (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c), 105 CMR 721.070(B) and the Department's manual).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What happens if the pharmacist does not notify the DEA when the follow-up never arrives?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The failure voids the authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to have dispensed without a written prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A written follow-up arrives on an ordinary prescription pad. What is the format problem, and what does it mean for the emergency dispensing?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires a written prescription, where state and federal law permit one, to carry the practitioner's signature and to be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid under 105 CMR 721.040(A), so it is not a follow-up delivered in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4), and the pharmacist's DEA-notification duty answers a failure to deliver one that complies.

quick_review.text: In a defined emergency a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II substance on a practitioner's oral authorization, limited to the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, with a reasonable effort to identify a prescriber who is not known to the pharmacist.
Outside paragraph (d), 21 CFR 1306.11(a) permits a Schedule II drug to be dispensed only pursuant to a written prescription signed by the practitioner.

On Massachusetts facts both definitions must be satisfied: 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens the oral route only in a 21 CFR 290.10 emergency situation, and 105 CMR 721.060(B) opens its route only in case of a 105 CMR 721.010 Emergency Situation.

The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing with everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature; 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) allows entry into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead.

A Massachusetts Emergency Situation is itself an enumerated ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), one of those M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish, which is why the follow-up runs on the exception route rather than the 2-day electronic clause.

105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the Massachusetts follow-up as seven business days after authorizing the emergency orally transmitted prescription, requires Authorization for Emergency Dispensing on its face, and requires it to comply with federal and state law; the Department's manual states the same seven business days.

The Massachusetts texts count differently: the statute's exception route is not more than 7 days for a written follow-up and the regulation not more than seven business days for a written or electronic one, so a follow-up delivered within 7 days meets both.

Federal law requires the follow-up within 7 days after the emergency oral authorization, and because 105 CMR 721.070(B) states its own period subject to any shorter federal one, seven days is the operative deadline.
If the follow-up does not arrive, the pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office.
A pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an ePrescribing exception or waiver.
A written follow-up must still satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and does not discharge the follow-up the practitioner owes.

decision_logic.condition: A practitioner offers an oral Schedule II authorization.
decision_logic.action: Work both definitions. The federal test in 21 CFR 290.10 adds a no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element and is keyed to a written prescription; the Massachusetts test in 105 CMR 721.010 is keyed to an electronic one and has a delay limb. On Massachusetts facts both must be satisfied before the oral route is open.

decision_logic.condition: The Massachusetts definition is satisfied but a federal element is not.
decision_logic.action: Do not dispense on the oral authorization. 21 CFR 1306.11(a) requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner outside paragraph (d), and an ePrescribing exception may let the prescriber issue that written prescription in Massachusetts.

decision_logic.condition: Both definitions are satisfied and the practitioner is not known to you.
decision_logic.action: Make a reasonable good faith effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered prescribing practitioner, then dispense no more than the amount adequate for the emergency period.

decision_logic.condition: You have dispensed on the oral authorization.
decision_logic.action: Immediately reduce it to writing, or enter it into a compliant electronic pharmacy system as 105 CMR 721.060(B)(2) allows, carrying every required element except the practitioner's signature.

decision_logic.condition: You are asked how long the practitioner has to deliver the follow-up.
decision_logic.action: Do not reach for the 2-day clause: it is the statute's rule where the practitioner has received no s. 23(h) exception, and the emergency is one of those exceptions. The statute's exception route gives not more than 7 days, 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 721.070(B) for seven business days or a shorter federal period, and 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) supplies 7 days from the oral authorization, which is the shortest of them.

decision_logic.condition: A written rather than electronic follow-up is used.
decision_logic.action: Check its face for Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, the date of the oral order and the indication that it documents an oral prescription; check the Massachusetts written-format requirements; and attach it to the oral prescription you reduced to writing.

decision_logic.condition: The follow-up arrives as an electronic prescription.
decision_logic.action: Annotate the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and the date of the oral order rather than filing a printout against the attachment rule.

decision_logic.condition: The federal 7-day period has run with no complying follow-up delivered.
decision_logic.action: Notify the nearest DEA office of the practitioner's failure to deliver.

ma_vs_federal.text: The two definitions of an emergency situation are not the same test, and on Massachusetts facts both must be met; a fact pattern that satisfies 105 CMR 721.010 but not 21 CFR 290.10 does not open the oral Schedule II route.

Massachusetts frames the emergency as a waiver of the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, leaving every other prescription requirement in force; federal law frames it as the exception to the signed written prescription that 21 CFR 1306.11(a) otherwise requires.
The seven-business-day Massachusetts count is not extra time: 105 CMR 721.070(B) states it subject to any shorter period federal law requires, and the 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) is shorter.

Federal law splits the handling of the follow-up by medium, attaching a paper one and annotating the record of an electronic one; 105 CMR 721.060(B)(5) states the attachment step with no annotation counterpart.

exceptions.text: Dispensing beyond the emergency period is not covered by the oral authorization and requires a paper or electronic prescription signed by the practitioner.
A central fill pharmacy is not authorized to prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization from a retail pharmacist or a practitioner.
Unlike the waiver route in 105 CMR 721.070(A)(3), which a practitioner applies for and receives, the emergency exception is not applied for; it attaches to the situation itself.
A mailed follow-up meets its period by the postmark rather than by the date the pharmacy receives it.

Outside the settings named in 21 CFR 1306.11(e) through (g), a faxed Schedule II prescription does not stand in for the original manually signed one, and both 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) provide for the written follow-up to be delivered in person or by mail.

timing_deadlines.event: Federal emergency oral Schedule II follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days after authorizing the emergency oral prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the shortest period reaching the prescription, so it is the operative deadline.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts regulation, follow-up under the ePrescribing exception route
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 7 business days, or such shorter period as federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.070(B) defers to the federal period rather than extending it, and the Department's manual states the same seven business days.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts regulation, emergency Schedule II follow-up stated directly
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 business days after authorizing the emergency orally transmitted prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the period for this pathway and requires the follow-up to comply with federal and state law.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts statute, written follow-up where the practitioner has received a commissioner's exception
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 7 days, or such shorter period as federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) counts 7 days where the regulation counts seven business days, so a follow-up delivered within 7 days meets both.

timing_deadlines.event: Missing follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Once the federal period has run
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office.

timing_deadlines.event: Pharmacist's own failure to notify
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No separate period; the consequence attaches to the omission
timing_deadlines.consequence: The authority to have dispensed without a written prescription is voided.

forms_records.text: The oral prescription is immediately reduced to writing with every element 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the practitioner's signature; on Massachusetts facts it carries everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires and may be entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead of being written out.

What M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires on that writing is a list rather than a cross-reference: the name, address and registration number of the practitioner and the name of any expressly authorized representative, the date of the prescription, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the serial number the dispensing pharmacy assigns, the name of that pharmacy, the name and address of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any cautionary statements required, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. Section 20(b) adds the reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered practitioner where that practitioner is not known to the pharmacist.
The follow-up bears the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order on its face.

On Massachusetts facts the follow-up also indicates that it is issued to document an oral prescription, which M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires of an electronic or written follow-up and 105 CMR 721.070(B) of a written one, and which the Department's manual states for every emergency follow-up.

On receipt the pharmacist attaches a paper follow-up to the oral prescription earlier reduced to writing, and annotates the record of an electronic follow-up with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.

A written follow-up must carry the practitioner's signature and satisfy 105 CMR 721.020(F), which governs written prescriptions where state and federal law permit them: transmitted by facsimile or similar technology, or written on a tamper-resistant form. Because 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) provide for the written prescription to be delivered in person or by mail, and because outside 21 CFR 1306.11(e) through (g) a faxed Schedule II prescription does not replace the original manually signed one, the tamper-resistant form is the route that fits this follow-up.

A prescription in a format that does not conform is invalid under 105 CMR 721.040(A), so it is not a follow-up delivered in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4), and the pharmacist's DEA-notification duty answers the practitioner's failure to deliver one that complies.

role_duties.duty: Determine the three federal emergency elements, act within the Massachusetts Emergency Situation, and cause the follow-up prescription bearing the required face notations to be delivered within the period.
Limit the quantity to the emergency period, make a reasonable effort to identify a prescriber who is not known to you, and reduce the order to writing immediately.
Notify the nearest DEA office when the follow-up is not delivered, understanding that omitting the notification voids the authority relied on to dispense.
Do not refuse an otherwise valid oral prescription for inability to confirm the practitioner's exception status; 105 CMR 721.070(C) imposes no such verification duty.

common_traps.text: Answering two days on a Massachusetts emergency oral question applies the statute's no-exception clause to a prescription that is always issued under an ePrescribing exception.
Answering seven business days treats the Massachusetts count as extra time, when 105 CMR 721.070(B) states it subject to the shorter federal period.

Reading the Massachusetts gate as the whole test: the federal elements are separate, and an electronic-prescribing outage does not establish the federal element, which asks about a written prescription.
Carrying the federal no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element into the Massachusetts test, or the Massachusetts delay limb into the federal one, mixes two definitions that differ.
Knowing the DEA notification duty without its consequence leaves the candidate unable to say what turns on the pharmacist's omission.
Treating an emergency oral authorization as covering continued therapy overlooks that dispensing beyond the emergency period needs a signed prescription.
Refusing a prescription because the practitioner's exception status cannot be confirmed invents a verification duty the regulation does not impose on the pharmacist.
Naming two face items on Massachusetts facts drops the indication that the follow-up is issued to document an oral prescription.
Accepting a faxed copy as the delivered Schedule II follow-up overlooks that outside 21 CFR 1306.11(e) through (g) federal law looks for the original manually signed prescription.

sections.title: Massachusetts Pharmacist Continuing Education
sections.topic: Licensure / Pharmacist continuing education under 247 CMR 4.00
sections.subtopic: The annual requirement, its practice-specific subject overlays, what may supply the hours, and how completion is proved
learning_objectives: State the cycle total, the annual minimum and the sworn statement that carries them to the Board at renewal.
Apply the three structural limits on the annual minimum: the home-study ceiling, the bar on carry-over and the daily ceiling.
Identify which practice-specific subject overlay attaches to a registrant, and whether it is measured per calendar year or per renewal cycle.
Distinguish the two routes to authorized-provider status and the two separate 30-day clocks in the provider process.
Separate the criteria the Board applies to a home-study program from those it applies to a live program.
List the five data elements a statement of credit must carry and the period for which it must be kept.
Name the three mechanisms that relieve a registrant of the requirement and the condition attached to each.
State what a random audit requires of a selected licensee, by when, and the statutory consequence of missing it.

orientation.text: Continuing education in Massachusetts is a condition precedent to renewing a personal registration rather than a formality that follows it. 247 CMR 4.03(1) draws the requirement from M.G.L. c. 112, § 24A, and 247 CMR 4.03(2) states the consequence flatly: no registrant is eligible for renewal of a personal registration without completion of the requisite number of contact hours. The architecture underneath that sentence is a two-year renewal cycle measured in calendar years. 247 CMR 4.03(3) has the registrant submit, with the renewal application, a statement signed under the penalties of perjury that a minimum of 40 contact hours has been satisfactorily completed, and 247 CMR 4.03(4) requires a minimum of 20 contact hours in each calendar year of that cycle. So the 40-hour figure is a cycle total proved by a sworn statement at renewal, while the 20-hour figure is the annual floor that has to produce it. Every count in this area is in contact hours, and 247 CMR 2.00 defines the unit: a contact hour is a minimum of 50 minutes, or the equivalent as determined by the Board, of satisfactory participation in a Board-approved program of continuing education, and ten contact hours make one continuing education unit.

Three structural limits stop a registrant from assembling those hours in any convenient way. 247 CMR 4.03(4)(b) allows no more than 15 contact hours per calendar year acquired through home study and other mediated instruction to be applied toward the 20-hour annual minimum, which leaves at least five hours a year that have to come from somewhere else; the cap limits what may be applied, not what may be taken. 247 CMR 4.03(5) forbids carrying contact hours from one calendar year into another. 247 CMR 4.03(7) forbids earning more than eight contact hours of continuing education in a calendar day, and it says nothing about delivery format, so it binds a live conference exactly as it binds home study. Read together these defeat the end-of-cycle catch-up: a registrant who earns 40 hours in one year of the cycle has still failed the other year, and no single day can be stretched to close a shortfall however long the program runs. What counts as home study is itself a defined term. 247 CMR 2.00 describes home study and other mediated instruction as continuing education activities that do not provide for direct interaction between faculty and participants, such as audio tapes, video tapes, cable television, computer assisted instruction, journal articles and monographs, and a live program as one that provides for that direct interaction, including lectures, symposia, live teleconferences and workshops. A live teleconference therefore counts as live and does not draw on the 15-hour ceiling.

247 CMR 4.03(4) then allocates subject matter inside the annual requirement it has just stated. Under 4.03(4)(a) every registrant owes at least two contact hours per calendar year in the area of pharmacy law. The remaining allocations attach to what the registrant does or to where the registrant practises. Under 4.03(4)(c) a registrant who oversees or is directly engaged in the practice of sterile compounding, or who practises in a pharmacy licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, § 39G or § 39I, must complete at least five contact hours per calendar year in sterile compounding. Under 4.03(4)(d) the figure is three contact hours per calendar year in complex non-sterile compounding for a registrant who oversees or is directly engaged in it or who practises in a § 39H pharmacy. Under 4.03(4)(e) a registrant who oversees or is engaged in the administration of vaccines must complete at least one contact hour on the topic of immunizations during the two-year renewal cycle, which is the one overlay measured over the cycle rather than the year.

The two compounding overlays behave differently from each other in one respect that the regulation's own grammar settles. Each of 247 CMR 4.03(4)(c) and (d) states its trigger disjunctively and then states its requirement once, so a registrant who both oversees sterile compounding and practises in a § 39G pharmacy has met two triggers for a single five-hour requirement and still owes five hours, not ten. But (c) and (d) are separate subject requirements in separate subsections, so a registrant who oversees sterile compounding and also oversees complex non-sterile compounding owes the five and the three together. The distinction worth carrying is between duplicate triggers for one overlay, which do not multiply it, and distinct overlays, which accumulate.

Hours count because of where they come from, and 247 CMR 4.04 governs that. A request for provider authorization, or for approval of a program from an authorized provider, must be submitted to the Board no less than 30 days in advance of the date of the proposed program's presentation. The Board may authorize the Executive Director or a designee to grant or deny those requests, and a provider whose request is denied may appeal to the full Board by written petition submitted within 30 days of the notice of denial. Those two 30-day periods run from different events and are easy to conflate. Alongside the application route, 247 CMR 4.04(5) supplies a recognition route: a person or agency who submits documentation acceptable to the Board of having received current program approval from, and being in good standing with, either the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education or the American Medical Association CME Category 1 is considered an authorized provider. The definition of a Board-approved program adds a discretionary source: the Board may, within its discretion, accept comparable continuing education hours approved by other Boards of Pharmacy.

247 CMR 4.05 sets what the program itself has to look like, and it asks different things of the two delivery formats. Under 4.05(3) a program intended for home study or other mediated instruction shall be developed by a professional group, follow a logical sequence, involve the learner by requiring an active response to materials and provide feedback, contain a test to indicate progress and to verify completion of the program, and supply a bibliography for continued study. Under 4.05(4) a live program shall involve direct interaction between the faculty and participants, and the faculty should possess the appropriate credentials related to the discipline being taught. Under 4.05(7) evaluation runs in both directions: provision shall be made for evaluating the participants' attainment of the stated learner objectives, and participants shall be given the opportunity to evaluate faculty, learning experiences, instructional methods, facilities and educational resources used for the program. Not everything in 4.05 turns on format. The application for each program states the qualifications of the faculty preparing and teaching it under 4.05(1)(j); 4.05(5) requires education methods appropriate to the program's objectives and designed on principles of adult education, with sufficient time for each activity and adequate facilities and resources; and 4.05(6) requires the faculty of any intended program to present documentation satisfactory to the Board of competence to teach its content and of knowledge of the principles of adult education.

Two further routes produce contact hours without sitting through someone else's program. Under 247 CMR 4.07 a registered pharmacist who is a Board-approved continuing education instructor receives credit for the program taught on a one-time basis annually, so teaching the same program four times in a year yields one credit rather than four. Under 247 CMR 4.08 a registered pharmacist who enrols in a postgraduate pharmacy curriculum, a postgraduate pharmacy program or a Board-approved postgraduate medical program is awarded contact hours for satisfactory completion of each course within it, but only on two conditions read together: the sponsor or co-sponsor must be a Board-authorized or ACPE-accredited provider of continuing professional education, and the course must provide instruction in pharmacy, pharmaceutical sciences, pharmacy practice or pharmacy law.

Completion has to be provable, and 247 CMR 4.06 says with what. A pharmacist shall maintain documentation or a statement of credit demonstrating successful completion for a period of at least two years from the date of completion, and that period runs from the date of the course rather than from the renewal that the course fed. The documentation must contain five things: the name of the authorized provider, the participant's name, the title and number of the continuing education program, the date of completion of the program, and the number of contact hours earned. A bare attendance list or a diary entry is not that document. 247 CMR 4.06(2) then requires the pharmacist to provide it to the Board upon request and in response to random audits, which is the point at which the sworn renewal statement under 247 CMR 4.03(3) is tested against something other than the registrant's own word. The audit itself comes from statute. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24A directs the Board to audit randomly selected renewed licences by sending the selected licensees a request for documentation evidencing completion of the required contact hours, and to post the name and date of licensees included in an audit on its website. It also fixes the consequence: a licensee who is not in compliance with the contact hour requirements, or who fails to provide the requested documentation within 7 days of receiving the request, shall be fined not more than $1,000.

Relief from the requirement comes through three defined mechanisms, none of which is informal hardship. 247 CMR 4.03(8) provides that a registrant is not required to complete continuing education in the calendar year in which the registrant has graduated from an approved college or school of pharmacy. 247 CMR 4.03(6) covers the registrant who failed to complete the requisite hours, and also the registrant who is unable because of a physical disability to conform to the home-study limitation: that registrant submits to the Board a detailed statement, signed under the penalties of perjury, setting forth the extenuating circumstances with detail and specificity, and the Board then determines whether a renewal shall be granted and notifies the applicant of its determination and reasons. 247 CMR 4.02(8), applying M.G.L. c. 112, § 1B(c), keeps the registration of a registrant engaged in active service in the armed forces valid until 90 days following release from active duty, and disapplies the continuing education requirement for the biennial cycle immediately preceding December 31st of an even-numbered year where the registrant is in active service after October 1st of that year.
